articles.title: Node.js Multipart Object Storage for Private AI-Generated Images in Production
articles.excerpt: Short answer: use a private object-storage bucket with multipart upload, and make the object key tenant-scoped. For a B2B SaaS system processing receipts and retaining original AI-generated images, th…
articles.body: Short answer: use a private object-storage bucket with multipart upload, and make the object key tenant-scoped. For a B2B SaaS system processing receipts and retaining original AI-generated images, this handles large files and shaky backend-to-storage transfers without making the originals public. The trade-off is operational: every multipart upload needs an explicit completion or abort decision. Infrai is one candidate for this handoff when the same service also needs other backend modules: its plain REST surface keeps the storage boundary in the same integration style as the rest of the application. Start with the tenant boundary The database should create the receipt record before the first byte moves.

articles.title: Healthtech DNS Record Control: CNAME Exclusivity Checks Before Hostname Alerts
articles.excerpt: Consider a healthtech on-call page: a patient portal hostname appears to resolve intermittently after an operator adds a DNS record through the internal admin console. The change log says the request…
articles.body: Consider a healthtech on-call page: a patient portal hostname appears to resolve intermittently after an operator adds a DNS record through the internal admin console. The change log says the request completed. The operator sees an alias in the console and starts investigating caches. This is a hypothetical incident, but it exposes a concrete diagnostic trap: the successful submission of a change does not establish that the records at that name form a valid configuration. Short answer: a CNAME cannot coexist with other records at the same name. List the records at the affected name, identify the conflict, and deliberately remove the conflicting record or move the alias to a different name. Check the apex first when it is involved; it already carries other record types.

articles.body: In this blog post, we will delve into the basic framework and development process of eBPF (Extended Berkeley Packet Filter). eBPF is a powerful network and performance analysis tool that runs on the Linux kernel, providing developers with the ability to dynamically load, update, and run user-defined code at kernel runtime. This enables developers to implement efficient, secure kernel-level network monitoring, performance analysis, and troubleshooting functionalities. This article is the second part of the eBPF Tutorial by Example, where we will focus on how to write a simple eBPF program and demonstrate the entire development process through practical examples. Before reading this tutorial, it is recommended that you first learn the concepts of eBPF by studying the first tutorial.

articles.title: A 1 mm hole doubles the stress in a spinning disk: checking the textbook result with FEM
articles.excerpt: Spin a solid disk and the highest stress sits at the centre. Drill a hole there, even a tiny one, and the stress at the edge of the hole is about twice that. It does not shrink toward the solid-disk v…
articles.body: Spin a solid disk and the highest stress sits at the centre. Drill a hole there, even a tiny one, and the stress at the edge of the hole is about twice that. It does not shrink toward the solid-disk value as the hole gets smaller. I checked this in NovaSolver Studio's structural solver with a CD-sized polycarbonate disk (120 mm across, 1.2 mm thick) spinning at 10,000 rpm. I solved a solid disk and five centre holes from 1 mm to 15 mm radius, and compared all six with the rotating-disk formulas. The formulas For a thin disk of outer radius R, density ρ and Poisson's ratio ν spinning at angular speed ω, the plane-stress solution gives the hoop (circumferential) stress.

articles.title: IAM for Growing Mid-Sized Companies
articles.excerpt: The question usually turns up in a security questionnaire from a big customer, or in the first audit: "Can you show who has access to what?" At a company of a few hundred people, quite often nobody ca…
articles.body: The question usually turns up in a security questionnaire from a big customer, or in the first audit: "Can you show who has access to what?" At a company of a few hundred people, quite often nobody can. Most companies between 100 and 1,000 people already do half of this. Someone disables accounts when people leave. Someone keeps an eye on who has admin. But it isn't written down, it depends on who's around that week, and there's no record of it happening. A handful of habits, done in the right order, plus evidence that you kept them, gets you most of the way. SailPoint and a six-month project can wait. You've probably outgrown the ad-hoc version if a few of these sound familiar. Nobody can list every app the company uses, let alone who's in each one.

articles.body: When a web app feels sluggish in production or fails intermittently during a multi-step checkout flow, a browser HTTP Archive ( .har ) capture contains the ground truth. Yet most developers only open .har files to glance at status codes, missing two massive productivity wins: Automated 7-Phase Network Bottleneck Diagnostics (distinguishing DNS/TLS handshakes from HTTP/1.1 connection pool starvation and backend TTFB stalls). Instant Replay Code Generation (converting the exact filtered network sequence into a runnable Playwright E2E test , a k6 load test script , or an OpenAPI 3.1 schema ). Let's look at how the HAR 1.2 timing specification works under the hood and how to transform raw network traces into executable tests. 1.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 10, 2013: Europe's GOCE satellite, the 'Ferrari of space,' fell out of orbit after mapping Earth's gravity field
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 10, 2013, Europe's GOCE satellite fell to Earth after four years in orbit mapping the planet's gravitational field. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 10, 2013, Europe's GOCE satellite fell to Earth after four years in orbit mapping the planet's gravitational field. GOCE, its name was short for Gravity field and steady-state Ocean Circulation Explorer, launched in 2009 on a mission to map Earth's gravity like never before. But despite that successful mission, it was doomed in 2013 when it ran out of fuel . At the time, controllers weren't sure where GOCE would fall back to Earth . Some people worried that it might crash into a populated area. However, the small spacecraft broke up in the atmosphere and didn't cause any property damage. It disintegrated about 50 miles above the Falkland Islands in the South Atlantic Ocean. The European Space Agency called the mission a success. GOCE lasted far longer than expected.

articles.body: Astronomers have solved the mystery of an extrasolar planet, or exoplanet, that "disappeared" after seven years of observations. New research suggests that the planet hasn't vanished at all, but has been dragged off its orbit by an unseen planet. The exoplanet , designated TOI-2535 b, is located around 1,000 light-years away. TOI-2535 b was routinely observed with NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite ( TESS ) space telescope for seven years between April 2019 and March 2026 as it completed its 8.25-Earth day orbit of its parent star. That's 10 times quicker than the orbit of Mercury around the sun and means this blisteringly hot planet is classed as a " hot Jupiter ." However, something strange happened started to happen as astronomers observed the distant world.
